newsitem.title: UK: Derivatives use by corporate treasurers on the rise.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives use by corporate treasurers on the rise.

text.p: Despite memories of Barings' collapse, more and more corporate treasurers are expected to use exchange-traded derivatives as they hone their financial skills, top industry figures said on Tuesday.
"Corporate use of derivatives will go on rising and I hope user expertise will improve," said Jeremy Wagener, director general of Britain's Association of Corporate Treasurers.
"There will be the periodic disaster but I don't think they will threaten the system systematically," he said.

Speakers at the seminar said however that most small companies were still reluctant to try out derivatives, even to hedge their currency and commodity risks. Instead, they resorted to natural hedges or OTC (over the counter) products.

Kate Barker, chief economic advisor at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said this partly stemmed from a misjudgement of costs and benefits in derivatives, and lack of expertise in most company boards to deal with sophisticated products that are on offer.
Some companies also had shareholder pressure to keep risks diversified, Barker said.
"It's odd that their use is not more widespread," she added.

Anthony Belchambers, chief executive of the Futures and Options Association (FOA), said despite the increased media attention on the dangers of derivatives following the Barings scandal, losses to institutional investors had actually been few in number.
"It's not a product problem. It's a people problem," said Belchambers. "Those losses have not really fazed at all those people who use them. But they have fazed potential users," he noted.
Barings collapsed in February 1995 after a trader, Nick Leeson, lost some $1.3 billion on unauthorised derivatives trades.
Wagener said treasurers should recognise the difference between hedging and speculating, and understand the appetite for risk within the corporate culture.
"Any corporate that doesn't recognise this is heading for trouble," he said.
Few companies used LIFFE (London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange) directly, but their risks were laid off indirectly with the exchange through brokers, Wagener said.

Corporate leaders cautiously welcomed the extended regulatory powers given to Britain's SIB (Securities and Investments Board). The new Labour government has shifted banking regulation to the SIB from the Bank of England.
"As always, the devil will be in the detail," said Wagener.
"(But) I quite like the idea of creative tension between two different regulators with slightly different views. Out of that might come a less opaque solution," he added.
